questions.q: In standard SQL, in which order are these clauses logically evaluated?
options: WHERE, FROM, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT
FROM, SELECT, WHERE, LIMIT, ORDER BY
FROM, WHERE, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
questions.why: Rows are gathered and filtered before the SELECT list is computed, which is why WHERE can't use a column alias defined in SELECT (ORDER BY can).

questions.q: `SELECT * FROM runs WHERE loss = NULL` returns how many rows?
options: None, because comparing with NULL gives unknown; use `IS NULL`
All rows with a missing loss
questions.why: Any comparison with NULL is unknown, not true, so WHERE drops every row. `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` test for missing values.

questions.q: A leaderboard query uses `ORDER BY score DESC`. Two models tie. What decides their order?
options: Nothing guaranteed; add a tie-breaker such as `, model_name`
Alphabetical order of the first column
questions.why: SQL makes no promise about the order of rows that compare equal. A deterministic leaderboard needs a second sort key.

questions.q: Page 3 of a feed with 20 items per page uses which clause?
questions.why: Pages 1 and 2 cover 40 rows, so page 3 skips 40. Large offsets are slow (the database still reads the skipped rows); keyset pagination on the last seen key scales better.

questions.q: `SELECT DISTINCT item, label FROM t` removes what?
questions.why: DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row. Two rows with the same item but different labels both stay.

questions.q: What does `SELECT 7 / 2` return in PostgreSQL and SQLite?
questions.why: Both operands are integers, so the result is an integer. Cast one side (`7.0 / 2` or `CAST(7 AS REAL) / 2`) to get 3.5.

questions.q: Which WHERE clause finds the validation rows where the model was wrong and confident (probability at least 0.9)?
options: `WHERE split = 'val' OR pred <> label AND prob >= 0.9`
`WHERE split = 'val' AND pred <> label AND prob >= 0.9`
questions.why: All three conditions must hold. In the second option AND binds tighter than OR, so it returns every validation row plus confident mistakes from other splits.

questions.q: `SELECT name AS n FROM t WHERE n LIKE 'a%'` fails in most databases. Why?
options: The alias `n` isn't available yet when WHERE runs
questions.why: WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list, so it must use the original column name. Repeat the expression or wrap the query in a subquery.

questions.q: `runs` has 100 rows; 10 reference a `model_id` missing from `models`. How many rows does `runs INNER JOIN models` return, assuming model ids are unique?
questions.why: An inner join keeps only rows with a match on both sides. A LEFT JOIN from runs would keep all 100 with NULL model columns.

questions.q: You LEFT JOIN `datasets` to `licenses` and filter `WHERE licenses.status = 'approved'`. What happens to datasets with no license?
options: They are dropped, because the WHERE turns the join into an inner join
They are kept with NULL status
questions.why: For unmatched rows `status` is NULL, and `NULL = 'approved'` is not true. Put the condition in the ON clause to filter licenses while keeping every dataset.

questions.q: A self join pairs runs with identical hyperparameters: `FROM runs a JOIN runs b ON a.cfg = b.cfg`. How do you avoid pairing a run with itself and listing each pair twice?
questions.why: `<>` removes self-pairs but still returns both (a, b) and (b, a). Requiring `a.run_id < b.run_id` keeps exactly one ordering.

questions.q: How many rows does `CROSS JOIN` of a 4-row learning-rate table and a 3-row batch-size table return?
questions.why: A cross join is the Cartesian product: every row of one table with every row of the other. That is how a hyperparameter grid is enumerated.

questions.q: Which query finds configs from the grid that have not been run yet?
options: `grid LEFT JOIN runs ON ... WHERE runs.run_id IS NULL`
`grid LEFT JOIN runs ON ... WHERE runs.run_id IS NOT NULL`
questions.why: The anti-join pattern keeps grid rows with no match, which show up with NULLs on the right side. `NOT EXISTS` is an equivalent alternative.

questions.q: Joining `orders → order_items → products → categories` returns duplicate order totals when you `SUM(orders.amount)`. Why?
options: Each order row is repeated once per item, so its amount is summed several times
questions.why: Joining to a many side fans out the one side. Aggregate items first, or sum only columns that live at the item level.

questions.q: What is the difference between `ON` and `WHERE` in an INNER JOIN?
options: WHERE can't reference the second table
ON filters after the join, WHERE before
None for the result; they only differ for outer joins
questions.why: For inner joins both conditions simply remove rows. For outer joins, ON decides what counts as a match (unmatched rows survive), while WHERE removes rows after NULLs are filled in.

questions.q: `a FULL OUTER JOIN b` keeps which rows?
options: All matches plus unmatched rows from both sides
questions.why: A full outer join is the union of a left and a right join. SQLite only added it in version 3.39; older versions emulate it with a UNION of two left joins.

questions.q: What does `COUNT(col)` count compared with `COUNT(*)`?
options: Non-NULL values of `col`, versus all rows
questions.why: Most aggregates ignore NULLs, including `COUNT(col)`. `COUNT(*)` counts rows regardless.

questions.q: `AVG(tokens)` over the values `100, NULL, 200` returns what?
questions.why: AVG ignores NULLs, so it averages the two known values. To treat missing as zero use `AVG(COALESCE(tokens, 0))`, which gives 100.

questions.q: Which clause filters groups by an aggregate, such as models with average test accuracy above 0.9?
questions.why: WHERE runs before grouping and can't see aggregates. HAVING runs after GROUP BY.

questions.q: "Consistently good" means every test run has `acc > 0.9`. Which HAVING clause expresses that?
questions.why: If the minimum is above the threshold, every run is. The average can pass with a few bad runs.

questions.q: How do you count true positives per model in one GROUP BY query?
options: `SUM(CASE WHEN pred = 1 AND label = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`
`WHERE pred = 1 AND label = 1` plus `COUNT(*)`, alongside the other cells
questions.why: Conditional aggregation computes several counts in one pass. `COUNT(expr)` counts every non-NULL result, including false ones, so it doesn't work. Filtering with WHERE removes the rows the other cells need.

questions.q: Total spend per country is the sum of per-user totals. Which shape is right?
options: `GROUP BY user, country` and stop there
Aggregate per user in a subquery, then group that by country
questions.why: Two-level aggregation needs two GROUP BYs, typically with a CTE or subquery. `SUM(DISTINCT ...)` silently drops users who spent the same amount.

questions.q: Which SELECT is invalid with `GROUP BY model` in standard SQL?
questions.why: Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. `region` is neither, so it has no single value per model. SQLite accepts it and picks an arbitrary row, which is a classic silent bug.

questions.q: `SUM(x)` over a group where every `x` is NULL returns what?
questions.why: With no non-NULL inputs, SUM has nothing to add and returns NULL. `COALESCE(SUM(x), 0)` gives zero.

questions.q: To keep the latest version of each record, which is right?
options: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY version DESC)` and keep row 1
`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id)` and keep row 1
`RANK() OVER (ORDER BY version DESC)` and keep rank 1
`MAX(version)` with `GROUP BY id`, selecting all columns
questions.why: Partitioning by id restarts the numbering per record. Selecting non-grouped columns alongside `MAX` isn't valid SQL, and the unpartitioned versions pick one row for the whole table.

questions.q: Scores `90, 90, 80`. What do `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` give for the 80?
questions.why: RANK leaves a gap after ties (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK doesn't (1, 1, 2). ROW_NUMBER would give 1, 2, 3 in an arbitrary tie order.

questions.q: How do window functions differ from GROUP BY?
options: They compute per-row results without collapsing rows
They are faster versions of GROUP BY
questions.why: A window function sees a set of related rows but returns a value for every input row, so details and aggregates can sit side by side.

questions.q: A running total of daily GPU-hours per team uses which expression?
options: `SUM(hours) OVER (PARTITION BY team ORDER BY day)`
questions.why: With an ORDER BY in the window, the default frame runs from the start of the partition to the current row, which is a running total.

questions.q: With `ORDER BY day` and two rows on the same day, the default window frame (`RANGE ... CURRENT ROW`) does what for a running sum?
options: Raises an error for duplicate days
Counts the rows in arbitrary order
Includes both same-day rows in each of their totals
questions.why: The default RANGE frame treats peers (rows with equal ORDER BY values) together. Use `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, or aggregate per day first, for a row-by-row total.

questions.q: `LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user ORDER BY ts)` returns what for each user's first event?
questions.why: There is no previous row inside the partition. That NULL is useful: it marks the start of the user's first session.

questions.q: Forward-filling missing readings in SQL is commonly done with which pattern?
options: A running `COUNT(value)` to form groups, then `MAX(value)` over each group
questions.why: `COUNT(value)` only increments on non-NULL rows, so each non-NULL reading and the NULLs after it share a group id; the group's single non-NULL value fills it. One LAG only fills single gaps.

questions.q: Can you use a window function in WHERE?
options: No; compute it in a subquery or CTE and filter outside
questions.why: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING. Some databases add a `QUALIFY` clause for this, but the portable approach is a subquery.

questions.q: `WHERE model_id NOT IN (SELECT model_id FROM evals)` returns no rows at all. What is the likely cause?
options: The subquery returns too many rows
The subquery returns a NULL, which makes every `NOT IN` unknown
questions.why: `x NOT IN (a, NULL)` means `x <> a AND x <> NULL`, and the second part is never true. `NOT EXISTS` doesn't have this trap.

questions.q: A recursive CTE for model lineage has an anchor and a recursive part. What stops the recursion?
options: The recursive part returns no new rows
questions.why: Each iteration joins the previous results to the table; when nothing new is found, the recursion ends. Cycles in the data need a depth limit or a visited path to avoid looping.

questions.q: In a recursive CTE, why is `UNION` sometimes preferred over `UNION ALL`?
options: `UNION ALL` isn't allowed in recursive CTEs
It removes duplicate rows, which can stop infinite loops on cyclic data
questions.why: `UNION ALL` keeps every row and is cheaper, but on a graph with cycles it can revisit rows forever; `UNION` discards rows already produced.

questions.q: To sort rows by a custom order `high, medium, low`, which ORDER BY works?
options: `ORDER BY CASE band WHEN 'high' THEN 1 WHEN 'medium' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END`
questions.why: Text sorts alphabetically (high, low, medium). Mapping each value to a number with CASE gives any order you want.

questions.q: A CASE expression without ELSE returns what when no branch matches?
questions.why: Missing ELSE means ELSE NULL. That can silently drop rows from later comparisons, so add an explicit ELSE when it matters.

questions.q: Weekly active users: which expression groups timestamps by week in PostgreSQL?
questions.why: `date_trunc` keeps the year, so weeks from different years don't merge. `EXTRACT(week ...)` gives a week number that repeats every year. In SQLite, `strftime('%Y-%W', ts)` plays the same role.

questions.q: To count distinct users per week, which aggregate do you use?
questions.why: A user active several times in a week should count once. `COUNT(user_id)` counts events.

questions.q: Normalising emails, which query splits `Name@Example.COM` into a lowercased local part and domain in SQLite?
questions.why: SQLite has no split function; `instr` finds the `@` position and `substr` slices around it. Lowercasing after splitting handles mixed-case domains.
